sources.note: Nothing for Kenaboi: Benjamin treats it as the last-recorded 'generically Malay' (non-Aslian) Peninsular variety, since absorbed into Temuan. The volume's only stress statement (p. 187, quoting Dunn et al. 2011: in most Aslian languages the final syllable 'always receives stress') is family-level, does not name Kenaboi, and Benjamin does not class Kenaboi as Aslian.

sources.citation: Wilkinson, R. J. 1910. The aboriginal tribes. (Papers on Malay Subjects.) Kuala Lumpur: Printed at the F.M.S. Government Press. ('Hervey's Kenaboi', pp. 37-39.)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No phonology content. pp. 37-38: Hervey 'took down on two occasions from wandering Sakai calling themselves Orang Kenaboi vocabularies that show no affinity to any other language in the world.. a most careful investigation has failed to confirm them. The people who live in the Kenaboi valley.. supplied vocabularies of their language, which turns out to be Mantra. Nine vocabularies in all have been collected.. yet none of these vocabularies bear out his informants' statements. Under the circumstances we must suspend judgment.' Nothing on accent, stress or tone.

sources.citation: Skeat, W. W. & C. O. Blagden. 1906. Pagan Races of the Malay Peninsula, vol. 2. London: Macmillan. (Kenaboi subdivision pp. 403-405; Comparative Vocabulary appendix, 'Accent' p. 773)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing Kenaboi-specific. p. 405: for Kenaboi 'no grammatical information whatever is available'. p. 773 ('Accent'), a blanket remark across all the Peninsula aboriginal wordlists: 'The data with regard to accent and emphasis are very meagre.. As a rule, the accent in all the aboriginal dialects appears to fall on the final syllable. This is most marked, however, in Sakai.. but the tendency is also traceable in Jakun, even in words of Malayan affinity.'
